newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Treu says next week could decide metal row.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Treu says next week could decide metal row.

text.p: Italian Labour Minister Tiziano Treu said on Saturday that a bitter and protracted dispute over metalworkers' pay could be resolved next week.
"We are working so that the next few days will really be decisive, but it's best to be cautious," Treu told reporters on the fringes of a conference in the northeastern town of Treviso.
"We're putting a lot of faith in Monday's meeting between business leaders and unions in the hope that it will..give a decisive push," Treu said.
The union bodies, CGIL, CISL and UIL, will meet the employers' umbrella group Confindustria on Monday.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi met leaders of the three main trades union confederations on Friday and a government statement issued afterwards noted a "fresh readiness to seek agreements".

CISL leader Sergio D'Antoni told reporters in Florence on Saturday that he put the chances of reaching a deal at more than 50 percent "if on Monday we can get rid of this atmosphere that has held up negotiations and all sides get down to talks".
The dispute, which affects some 1.7 million workers in a sector accounting for 40 percent of Italian industrial output, is expected to set the tone for pay deals in other sectors.
Metalworkers unions have already staged strikes to press their claims for increases in wage contracts for the 1996-98 period. The previous contracts ran out in June.

The government suggested in December that management should raise pay by an average 200,000 lire ($125) a month. Union leaders, who had sought a 230,000 lire rise, accepted but the main industry group Federmeccanica rejected it as inflationary.
It has stuck to its original 139,000 lire offer.
The dispute centres on the interpretation of a landmark wage deal in July 1993 between the labour confederations, Confindustria and the government, which scrapped automatic index-linked wage rises.

"We want a deal that protects the purchasing power of metalworkers," Sergio Cofferati, leader of the CGIL confederation, told reporters in Turin. But he said the unions were "willing to seek solutions to ease the cost on businesses".
